rules.permitted_development: A loft conversion can fall within Class B permitted development in England if the roof enlargement stays within the roof-space allowance, remains below the existing ridge and does not project beyond the principal roof slope facing a highway.

rules.height_rules: No part of the enlargement should rise above the highest part of the existing roof. Raising the ridge usually takes the scheme out of permitted development.
rules.depth_rules: Keep dormers and other roof projections within the roof-space allowance: up to 40 cubic metres on a terraced house or 50 cubic metres on a detached or semi-detached house, taking earlier roof enlargements into account.
rules.boundary_rules: Side-facing windows should be obscure glazed and non-opening below 1.7m, and rooflights or dormers that look directly into neighbouring rooms or gardens can still create overlooking issues.
rules.roof_rules: The enlargement must not project beyond the existing roof slope on the principal elevation facing a highway. Other than a hip-to-gable alteration, it should be set back at least 20cm from the eaves and should not create a balcony or roof terrace.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should be similar in appearance to the existing house so the roof works read as part of the original building rather than a bolt-on addition.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof enlargements and dormers in a conservation area face much closer control, especially on principal or highway-facing slopes and where the roofscape is sensitive.
restrictions.listed_building: Do not rely on standard householder permitted development rights for a listed building. Listed building consent is usually required for roof alterations or works affecting character, and planning permission may also be needed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove the normal roof-alteration fallback route in selected streets or heritage areas, so check the property's designation before relying on permitted development.

rules.permitted_development: A loft conversion can still fall within Class B in England, but in parts of this authority heritage controls or an Article 4 direction may remove that fallback route. Even where rights remain, the roof enlargement still has to stay within the roof-space allowance, below the ridge and off the principal roof slope facing a highway.

rules.height_rules: The basic height rule does not change in heritage-sensitive streets: nothing should exceed the existing ridge or highest roof point, and raising the roof will usually need permission.
rules.depth_rules: Keep dormers and other roof projections within the roof-space allowance: up to 40 cubic metres on a terraced house or 50 cubic metres on a detached or semi-detached house, taking earlier roof enlargements into account.
rules.boundary_rules: The usual privacy rules still apply: side-facing windows should be obscure glazed and non-opening below 1.7m, while tighter heritage streets can make overlooking and roofscape change more sensitive.
rules.roof_rules: The enlargement must not project beyond the existing roof slope on the principal elevation facing a highway. Other than a hip-to-gable alteration, it should be set back at least 20cm from the eaves and should not create a balcony or roof terrace.
rules.materials_rules: Material matching matters more in heritage-sensitive streets. The safest approach is to keep the new roof finish and detailing close to the existing house so the alteration reads as restrained work.
